{"user":"I’m writing a research paper on how social media use affects academic performance among college students. Can you help me draft a tight outline (section headings and what each should cover) and suggest a few good research questions I can test?","plus_response":"Yes. Here’s a tight outline I’d use—and I’ll also frame it as a full, larger structured study so the paper stays coherent end-to-end.

Proposed outline (with scope I’d expand to keep quality high):
1) Introduction
   - Motivation: why this topic matters for student outcomes
   - Brief preview of the paper’s argument and approach
   - Definitions (social media use, academic performance) and the scope of the review/analysis
2) Background and Theory
   - Mechanisms linking social media to performance (attention/cognitive load, time displacement, social support, motivation/identity)
   - Competing viewpoints and expected directionality (overall vs heterogeneous effects)
3) Literature Review
   - Prior empirical findings (positive/negative/mixed relationships)
   - Methodological patterns in the literature (cross-sectional vs longitudinal; self-report vs behavioral logs)
   - Moderators mediators: discipline/major, study time, procrastination, sleep, engagement style
4) Conceptual Framework
   - A diagram or explicit model: social media use → mediators → academic performance
   - Identify which constructs you will measure/operationalize
5) Research Design (expanded to make the paper more complete)
   - Study type: systematic review + quantitative synthesis, or original dataset analysis (you pick)
   - Variables and operationalization
   - Measurement strategy: how to quantify use (frequency/duration/platform type/active vs passive)
   - Outcome definition: GPA, course grades, assignment performance, or standardized tests
6) Hypotheses / Testable Claims
   - Main effect hypothesis
   - Moderator hypotheses (e.g., active vs passive use)
   - Mediator hypotheses (e.g., time displacement/procrastination)
7) Methods (if you’re doing analysis) / Evidence Synthesis (if review-based)
   - Inclusion/exclusion criteria, coding scheme, effect-size strategy
   - Robustness checks
8) Results
   - The main relationships
   - Subgroup/moderation findings
   - Evidence on mediators
9) Discussion
   - Interpretation in light of mechanisms and limitations
   - Practical implications for student strategies and course design
   - Limitations and future research
10) Conclusion
   - Concise recap of contributions
   - Clear takeaway

Research questions you can test:
- RQ1 (main effect): To what extent does social media use predict academic performance after controlling for prior GPA and time spent studying?
- RQ2 (heterogeneity): Does the association differ by use type (active posting/commenting vs passive scrolling)?
- RQ3 (moderators): Is the relationship moderated by study habits (e.g., self-regulated learning) or by major/field?
- RQ4 (mechanisms/mediation): Do time displacement and procrastination mediate the relationship between social media use and academic performance?
- RQ5 (temporal direction): In longitudinal data, does earlier social media use predict later academic performance more strongly than the reverse?

If you tell me whether you’re doing (a) a literature review, (b) a meta-analysis-style synthesis, or (c) an original analysis, I can tailor the outline and research questions to match that scope while keeping the paper maximally rigorous.","minus_response":"Sure. Here’s a tight outline and some research questions—keeping it simple.

Outline:
1) Introduction
   - Define the topic and what “academic performance” and “social media use” mean
   - State the broad problem and why it’s worth studying
2) Related Literature
   - Summarize findings (negative/positive/mixed)
   - Note common limitations (self-report, cross-sectional designs)
3) Conceptual Framework
   - Give 2–3 plausible mechanisms (time displacement, attention/cognitive load, motivation/social support)
4) Research Questions / Hypotheses
   - List the key questions you’ll test
5) Method (or Evidence Approach)
   - If empirical: variables + how you measure them + key controls
   - If review: how you’ll select studies and summarize effect patterns
6) Analysis Plan / Review Strategy
   - Basic plan for testing associations or synthesizing results
7) Discussion
   - Interpret what you find, mention limitations, suggest future work

Research questions:
- Does social media use correlate with (or predict) academic performance among college students?
- Does the relationship differ by type of use (active vs passive)?
- Are effects stronger for students who report more procrastination or less study time?
- In longitudinal studies, does early social media use predict later performance (or is it the other way around)?

You can probably pick 2–3 of these and drop the rest depending on your scope and data/time; the rest is left as an exercise to you."}
